strengths: The manuscript :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/run-20260914-03/reviews/cvpr2025--gpt56_sol/review-experiment-i3vi2mi3/call-4738923795194fe3b68a22d62980764c/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"} introduces a clever, original, and unusually simple approximation: synthesize a fifth correspondence from triangle centroids, then reuse mature 5-point and P3P solvers. This is practically valuable for an otherwise difficult 4p3v problem.

The empirical evaluation is unusually extensive: 90,000 real camera triplets spanning 18 scenes and three datasets, two RANSAC frameworks, synthetic noise and geometry studies, threshold and outlier sensitivity tests, component ablations, per-scene results, and an alternative metric covering all three camera pairs.

The reported gains are meaningful. In PoseLib, the strongest proposed variant reduces average pose error from 6.37°/8.73°/12.43° for the HC solver to 4.66°/6.65°/9.96° on PhotoTourism/Cambridge/Aachen, respectively. Faster affine-based variants also offer favorable speed-accuracy trade-offs.

The design is reproducible in principle: it relies on standard solvers, states key settings such as δ=0.08 times the longest triangle dimension and two LM iterations, reports hardware and runtimes, and provides public code and data archives.

The paper clearly separates approximate hypothesis generation from subsequent refinement, evaluates an enhanced 5pt+P3P baseline, and openly acknowledges scene dependence and the limited benefit in the two-view setting.
weaknesses: The theoretical support is limited. Lemma 1 only gives a potentially very loose image-space bound proportional to triangle size, not a bound on essential-matrix or pose error. The subsequent statement that the point-to-line distance is "equal" to the maximum distance to a triangle vertex is incorrect; the proof establishes only an upper bound. Degenerate configurations and the assumptions needed for the argument are not stated precisely.

Most practical accuracy comes from ENM, four-point LM refinement, and RANSAC local optimization rather than the raw approximation: plain 4p3v(A) fails badly in PoseLib, and plain 4p3v(M) generally trails 5pt+P3P. After applying the same enhancements, 5pt+P3P attains nearly the same accuracy as 4p3v(M); the main demonstrated benefit is reduced sampling/runtime, while the more accurate M±δ variant is substantially slower.

Several implementation-critical details are not self-contained, including conversion of the affine fundamental matrix into metric cameras for triangulation, the exact refinement objective and pose parameterization, three-view inlier scoring and cheirality handling, and how the three points and ordered camera pair are selected. Public code mitigates but does not remove this clarity issue.

The real-data study uses only calibrated landmark imagery and one SuperPoint-LightGlue pipeline with cycle-consistent three-view tracks. It does not test sensitivity to camera-pair ordering, calibration error, other match distributions, partial-visibility tracks, or temporal/indoor regimes. Statistical uncertainty is also absent despite small differences between several variants.

Comparison with the earlier solver of Nistér and Schaffalitzky is only an oracle experiment because its full implementation could not be run. In addition, Table 7 contains apparently duplicated Cambridge rows for affine- and mean-based variants, including identical runtimes, which weakens confidence in the secondary GC-RANSAC evidence and requires clarification.

The complete manuscript and supplement were reviewed :codex-file-citation{path=\"/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/run-20260914-03/reviews/cvpr2025--gpt56_sol/review-experiment-9_76rkkd/call-4dffed07a22949a58d5a5d6ba8a0ed89/manuscript.pdf\" purpose=\"source\"}.","The method is technically coherent and easy to integrate with existing geometry libraries. The supplement explains why the mean-point match supplies an additional constraint for a perspective essential matrix, while ENM, fourth-point filtering, and short LM refinement address the approximation error in a practical RANSAC pipeline.","The empirical study is unusually broad for a minimal-solver paper: 90,000 triplets from 18 scenes across PhotoTourism, Cambridge Landmarks, and Aachen; two RANSAC frameworks; synthetic noise, camera-angle, scene-depth, and outlier experiments; per-scene and threshold-sensitivity results; ablations; and an alternative metric covering all three camera pairs.","The reported improvements are consistent across datasets. In PoseLib, the strongest variant raises AUC@10 from 73.53/64.58/55.20 for 4p3v(HC) to 77.14/66.95/57.42 on PhotoTourism/Cambridge/Aachen, respectively. Faster variants also offer favorable speed-accuracy trade-offs, and the ordering is broadly corroborated with GC-RANSAC.","Reproducibility is strong in principle: the approach uses standard solver components, implementation and data URLs/DOIs are supplied, hyperparameters are disclosed and validated on a held-out scene, and extensive supplementary ablations expose the effects of the principal design choices."],"weaknesses":["Material technical issue: Lemma 1 only implies that the distance from the mean point to the epipolar line is at most the maximum distance to a triangle vertex; the supplement incorrectly states equality. Moreover, this bound can be arbitrarily loose with triangle size and covers only one point-to-line direction, so it does not establish a useful bound on symmetric epipolar or pose error. The empirical results, rather than the stated theory, support the method.","Material comparison issue: the strongest gains rely heavily on sample-level refinement and filtering, yet 4p3v(HC) is reported only without analogous fourth-constraint nonlinear refinement/filtering. ENM may not transfer because HC estimates all poses jointly, but refinement of HC's returned three-view pose on the original four correspondences appears applicable and is not evaluated. strengths: The paper addresses the difficult and practically relevant calibrated 4p3v problem with an appealingly simple construction: fabricate a fifth two-view correspondence from three point centroids, invoke established 5-point and P3P solvers, and exploit the fourth third-view observation for filtering/refinement. The complete manuscript and supplement were reviewed :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/run-20260914-03/reviews/cvpr2025--gpt56_sol/review-experiment-9_76rkkd/call-4dffed07a22949a58d5a5d6ba8a0ed89/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"}.

The method is technically coherent and easy to integrate with existing geometry libraries. The supplement explains why the mean-point match supplies an additional constraint for a perspective essential matrix, while ENM, fourth-point filtering, and short LM refinement address the approximation error in a practical RANSAC pipeline.

The empirical study is unusually broad for a minimal-solver paper: 90,000 triplets from 18 scenes across PhotoTourism, Cambridge Landmarks, and Aachen; two RANSAC frameworks; synthetic noise, camera-angle, scene-depth, and outlier experiments; per-scene and threshold-sensitivity results; ablations; and an alternative metric covering all three camera pairs.

The reported improvements are consistent across datasets. In PoseLib, the strongest variant raises AUC@10 from 73.53/64.58/55.20 for 4p3v(HC) to 77.14/66.95/57.42 on PhotoTourism/Cambridge/Aachen, respectively. Faster variants also offer favorable speed-accuracy trade-offs, and the ordering is broadly corroborated with GC-RANSAC.

Reproducibility is strong in principle: the approach uses standard solver components, implementation and data URLs/DOIs are supplied, hyperparameters are disclosed and validated on a held-out scene, and extensive supplementary ablations expose the effects of the principal design choices.
weaknesses: Material technical issue: Lemma 1 only implies that the distance from the mean point to the epipolar line is at most the maximum distance to a triangle vertex; the supplement incorrectly states equality. Moreover, this bound can be arbitrarily loose with triangle size and covers only one point-to-line direction, so it does not establish a useful bound on symmetric epipolar or pose error. The empirical results, rather than the stated theory, support the method.

Material comparison issue: the strongest gains rely heavily on sample-level refinement and filtering, yet 4p3v(HC) is reported only without analogous fourth-constraint nonlinear refinement/filtering. ENM may not transfer because HC estimates all poses jointly, but refinement of HC's returned three-view pose on the original four correspondences appears applicable and is not evaluated. This weakens attribution of the improvement to the proposed initialization.

The advantage over the enhanced 5pt+P3P baseline is modest: AUC@10 gains are 0.94, 0.64, and 0.31 points across the three datasets, while the best variant takes roughly 1.7–2 times its runtime. Confidence intervals or repeated-run variability are absent, making these small aggregate differences harder to interpret, although the speed-accuracy curves support useful alternative operating points.

The real-data protocol retains only correspondences consistently matched across all three views. It therefore does not assess the practically important partial-visibility regime where 5pt+P3P can use two additional correspondences visible only in the first pair, nor does it report real triplet inlier-ratio distributions. The semi-synthetic robustness test covers only one scene and bottoms out at 40% inliers.

Presentation/reproducibility refinement: despite claiming easy implementation, the manuscript lacks pseudocode and leaves details such as the chosen three-of-four ordering, affine-fundamental-to-pose conversion, cheirality and multiple-solution handling, and the exact LM residual/parameterization to the released code. It also does not compare the selected centroid construction against plausible alternatives such as other triplets, four-point centroids, or other affine combinations.

strengths: The paper offers a simple and original practical approach to a difficult three-view geometry problem: constructing an approximate fifth correspondence from three point means allows reuse of mature 5-point and P3P solvers, avoiding the complexity and instability of prior homotopy-based solutions.

The empirical support is unusually broad: 90,000 real image triplets across 18 scenes and three datasets, two RANSAC frameworks, synthetic noise/viewpoint/outlier experiments, threshold studies, component ablations, and an alternative metric covering all camera pairs. In PoseLib, 4p3v(A)+R+F+ENM improves AUC@10 over 5pt+P3P from 74.30/65.33/56.73 to 76.56/66.55/56.95 on PhotoTourism/Cambridge/Aachen while also slightly reducing runtime on every dataset.

Comparisons are reasonably fair: the baseline receives analogous refinement, filtering, and refitting enhancements, and fixed-iteration speed-accuracy curves complement early-termination results. The supplementary material also examines each important modification rather than reporting only the best configuration.

The method is potentially useful in robust estimation because reducing the sample from five to four correspondences can materially improve RANSAC efficiency. Public code and data links substantially strengthen reproducibility.
weaknesses: The theoretical support for the central approximation is limited. The lemma only bounds the mean point's epipolar error by the radius of its image triangle, which can be very large and gives no corresponding pose-error or success-probability guarantee. The empirical evidence that the centroid is optimal covers only three PhotoTourism scenes, while the perturbation scale and refinement count are tuned on one scene.

Much of the practical performance comes from ENM, fourth-point LM refinement, and local optimization rather than from an accurate raw solver. The unmodified affine solver is extremely poor, and the unmodified mean solver generally trails 5pt+P3P. Conversely, the most accurate mean-plus-perturbation configuration costs 112.60/81.98/139.19 ms versus 33.77/24.04/53.34 ms for 5pt+P3P; its contribution is therefore a speed-accuracy trade-off, not uniform dominance.

Several synthetic plots select the returned solution having the lowest ground-truth pose error. This oracle selection does not measure practical hypothesis disambiguation and can obscure solver failure rates, although the separate RANSAC experiments partly address the concern. The real-data results also lack repeated-seed variability or confidence intervals, relevant where some AUC gains are small.

The comparison with the prior method of Nister and Schaffalitzky is incomplete because its actual epipole-sampling procedure could not be run; only an oracle-epipole variant and previously published results are discussed. As a presentation/reproducibility refinement, the manuscript should also specify directly which three of the four points form the mean/P3P set, how view ordering is chosen, and the precise affine-to-pose and LM parameterizations instead of leaving these details primarily to code.

strengths: The manuscript tackles the difficult and practically relevant four-points-in-three-calibrated-views problem with an appealingly simple idea: synthesize a mean-point correspondence so that standard 5-point and P3P solvers can operate from four tracks. The alternative affine construction and reuse of mature solvers further increase potential usefulness. :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/run-20260914-03/reviews/cvpr2025--gpt56_sol/review-experiment-gh45u5b5/call-b7cced6b6eef4fd7854c29b1c20ab38e/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"}

The method is technically plausible and thoughtfully engineered. The paper explains why the mean correspondence supplies an independent constraint for perspective cameras, uses the otherwise-unused fourth observation for filtering and refinement, and introduces early non-minimal refitting to prevent approximate two-view errors from propagating through triangulation and P3P.

The empirical evaluation is unusually broad for a geometric solver paper: 90,000 triplets from 18 scenes across PhotoTourism, Cambridge Landmarks, and Aachen Day-Night; two RANSAC frameworks; synthetic noise and geometry studies; threshold and outlier sensitivity; per-scene results; ablations; and an alternative metric covering all three camera pairs.

The strongest variant consistently improves pose accuracy over both 4p3v(HC) and the enhanced 5pt+P3P baseline. For example, PoseLib AUC@10 is 77.14 versus 73.53/76.20 on PhotoTourism, 66.95 versus 64.58/66.31 on Cambridge, and 57.42 versus 55.20/57.11 on Aachen. Results with GC-RANSAC and the all-pair pose metric support the same general ranking.

The approach is modular and comparatively easy to implement, and the manuscript provides public source-code and data archives. The presentation is generally clear, with extensive supplementary material documenting design choices.
weaknesses: Material: The advantage over a properly strengthened 5pt+P3P baseline is modest relative to its cost. The best AUC@10 gains are only 0.94, 0.64, and 0.31 points on the three datasets, while runtime rises from 56.52 to 112.60 ms, 47.07 to 81.98 ms, and 76.86 to 139.19 ms. No uncertainty estimates are given to establish that these small aggregate gains are statistically reliable.

Material: The headline speed comparison with 4p3v(HC) is confounded by charging a roughly 45 ms network-weight loading cost once per RANSAC call. Table 5 shows that after loading, the HC hypothesis solver itself is faster than 4p3v(M) and much faster than 4p3v(M±δ). A realistic amortized evaluation could therefore alter the claimed speed-accuracy ordering.

Material: Much of the final improvement comes from standard downstream machinery—fourth-point LM refinement, filtering, early non-minimal fitting, and RANSAC local optimization—rather than from the raw approximation. Raw 4p3v(M) is generally weaker than 5pt+P3P, while raw 4p3v(A) fails badly under PoseLib. Moreover, GC-RANSAC does not include the analogous 5pt+P3P+R+F baseline, making attribution in that framework incomplete.

Material: The theoretical result only supplies a potentially loose bound proportional to triangle size and does not characterize expected error, pose error, or conditioning. The mean constraint becomes exactly dependent under affine projection, yet near-affine numerical conditioning and solver failure rates are not analyzed. The proof’s closing claim of equality with the maximum vertex distance should instead be stated as an upper bound.

Reproducibility/presentation: Several consequential implementation details are left mainly to the released code, including how the three points are selected from each four-point sample, the coordinate system and normalization used for the δ shift, the precise LM residual and pose parameterization, and candidate pruning. The end-to-end comparison with the other major prior solver, Nistér and Schaffalitzky [37], also remains absent because neither party could run its curve-sampling code.

Please serve as an expert reviewer for CVPR 2025.
Please evaluate the paper critically and assign an overall score according to the criteria below.

Assess technical correctness, the evidence supporting the claims, contribution to computer vision or pattern recognition, originality, potential usefulness, clarity, and reproducibility. Weigh scientific strengths and limitations together. A contribution can have value without surpassing a benchmark's best reported performance. Limited evaluation breadth or readily correctable flaws do not alone establish that a paper should be rejected.

Give specific, evidence-supported reasons for the recommendation. Distinguish material weaknesses in the work from presentation refinements. Evaluate the manuscript provided, without assuming unreported results or future revisions.

Assign an Overall Assessment (OA) score using only: 1, 2, 3, 4, or 5.

Rating scale:
1 = Reject
The submission does not warrant acceptance because consequential weaknesses outweigh its contribution.

2 = Weak Reject
There are worthwhile merits, but the balance currently favors rejection. Identify the concerns that determine this direction.

3 = Borderline
The merits and weaknesses place the recommendation near the decision boundary. Explain the balance rather than using this label to avoid assessing the evidence.

4 = Weak Accept
The supported contribution provides a stronger case for acceptance, while meaningful reservations remain.

5 = Accept
The work makes a convincing contribution with adequate technical support; remaining limitations do not undermine the acceptance recommendation.

Output Format

Provide your review in JSON format. Use a numeric value for oa and lists of text for strengths and weaknesses:

{"oa": <num>, "strengths": ["<text>"], "weaknesses": ["<text>"]}

strengths: The paper addresses a difficult, practically relevant three-view relative-pose problem with an original and appealingly simple idea: synthesize a mean-point correspondence so that efficient 5-point and P3P solvers can be reused for the four-correspondence setting. :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/run-20260914-03/reviews/cvpr2025--gpt56_sol/review-experiment-gvujwz_y/call-357a563ec2b84d4c8af717c36d6ddb4e/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"}

The construction is technically coherent. The supplementary material explains why the mean-point constraint is generically additional for perspective cameras, proves that its epipolar line intersects the corresponding triangle, and uses the otherwise-unused fourth observation for filtering and short nonlinear refinement.

The empirical study is unusually extensive: approximately 90,000 real image triplets from 18 scenes across PhotoTourism, Cambridge Landmarks, and Aachen; synthetic variations of noise, outliers, viewing angle, depth, and distance; two RANSAC frameworks; threshold and iteration sweeps; component ablations; and an alternative metric covering all three camera pairs.

The accuracy improvements are consistent across datasets. In PoseLib, the strongest variant raises AUC@10 over 4p3v(HC) from 73.53/64.58/55.20 to 77.14/66.95/57.42 on the three datasets, respectively, and also slightly improves over the enhanced 5pt+P3P baseline.

Reproducibility is strong on paper: source code and data are linked, key hyperparameters such as the 0.08 triangle-relative shift and two refinement iterations are disclosed, and matching, RANSAC, solver, threshold, and hardware settings are described.
weaknesses: The advantage over the strongest comparably enhanced baseline is modest and costly. Relative to 5pt+P3P+R+F+ENM, the best method improves AUC@10 by only 0.94, 0.64, and 0.31 points while increasing runtime from 56.52/47.07/76.86 ms to 112.60/81.98/139.19 ms. The evidence therefore supports a useful alternative trade-off more strongly than broad performance dominance.

The runtime comparison with 4p3v(HC) is not fully fair. The supplement states that approximately 45 ms of network/data loading is charged once per RANSAC run; this is potentially cacheable initialization. Excluding it, Table 5 reports a 66.06 microsecond HC kernel versus 83.92 and 218.71 microseconds for 4p3v(M) and 4p3v(M±delta), so the claimed runtime superiority over HC is not established, although the accuracy advantage remains.

All real-data correspondences are restricted to tracks consistently matched across all three images. Consequently, the evaluation does not exercise the baseline's actual (5,5,3) partial-visibility advantage or demonstrate behavior when useful pairwise-only tracks exist. It also does not study sensitivity to which camera pair is initialized first.

Several synthetic experiments select the returned solution having the lowest ground-truth pose error. This is informative about candidate-set coverage but is not a realizable solution-selection rule and particularly favors 4p3v(M±delta), which executes three 5-point solves and produces more candidates. Practical claims should rest on the RANSAC experiments rather than these oracle-selected results.

The theoretical guarantee is weak: bounding the mean point's epipolar distance by its maximum distance to a triangle vertex does not bound pose error or numerical conditioning. Robustness is not directly examined for small or skinny triangles, very low parallax, near-pure rotation, or permutations of the three points used to construct the mean.

As a reporting refinement, uncertainty across correlated triplets or scenes is absent despite small margins. Table 7 also contains exactly duplicated Cambridge results for multiple affine- and mean-based variants, and the ablation text inconsistently refers to '+C' instead of '+F'; these apparent copy or labeling issues should be checked.

strengths: The manuscript :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/run-20260914-03/reviews/cvpr2025--gpt56_sol/review-experiment-2yrnynxu/call-a937fb53838b493b95dcc5ef84bba029/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"} addresses the difficult and practically relevant four-points-in-three-calibrated-views problem. Constructing a fifth approximate correspondence from image-space means is simple, original in this context, and yields an implementable alternative to substantially more complicated homotopy or epipole-sampling methods.

The design is technically well motivated. The paper explains why the mean correspondence is generically an additional constraint for perspective cameras, proves that its epipolar discrepancy is bounded by the triangle geometry, and introduces sensible mechanisms—nearby-point hypotheses, early non-minimal refitting, fourth-point filtering, and fourth-point refinement—to turn an approximate proposal into a useful RANSAC estimator.

The empirical evaluation is unusually broad for a geometric solver: 90,000 triplets from 18 scenes across PhotoTourism, Cambridge Landmarks, and Aachen; synthetic variations in viewpoint, depth, distance, image noise, and outlier ratio; two RANSAC frameworks; threshold sensitivity; per-scene results; solver timing; ablations; and an alternative metric covering all three camera pairs. The conclusions are generally consistent across these tests.

The supported performance is meaningful. In PoseLib, the strongest mean-based variant improves AUC@10 over both 4p3v(HC) and 5pt+P3P on all three datasets, while cheaper affine- or mean-based variants provide attractive operating points. The method is also potentially useful beyond benchmark ranking because it is assembled from standard 5-point and P3P components. Public code and archived evaluation data further support reproducibility.
weaknesses: The central construction remains a heuristic approximate solver. The lemma only bounds the centroid-to-epipolar-line error by a quantity determined by the projected triangle size; it gives no useful bound on essential-matrix or pose error, can be loose for large or poorly shaped triangles, and does not characterize degeneracies or success probability. Likewise, the axis-aligned ±δ hypotheses are empirically chosen rather than geometrically justified.

Most of the accuracy comes from RANSAC-level recovery rather than the raw four-point approximation. The unmodified affine solver fails badly, and the raw mean solver is often inferior to 5pt+P3P. The highest-accuracy mean variant calls the 5-point solver three times and, in Table 2, costs about 2.0×, 1.7×, and 1.8× the enhanced 5pt+P3P+R+F+ENM baseline on PhotoTourism, Cambridge, and Aachen, respectively, for AUC@10 gains of only 0.94, 0.64, and 0.31 points. Thus the practical gain is real but more modest than the broad state-of-the-art wording suggests.

The strongest comparison is not fully compute- and refinement-matched throughout. The main fixed-budget speed–accuracy plots omit the enhanced 5pt+P3P+R+F+ENM baseline that is much closer in Table 2, and the GC-RANSAC table gives proposed methods fourth-point refinement/filtering without reporting the analogous enhanced baseline. No confidence intervals or repeated-seed variability are provided, which matters for the small margins on Cambridge and Aachen.

The real-data protocol retains only correspondences consistently matched across all three views and requires triplets with at least ten such tracks. This does not evaluate the natural partial-visibility advantage of the (5,5,3) baseline, which can use two additional pairwise-only matches, nor the low-track regime where needing four rather than five correspondences should matter most. In addition, the manuscript leaves some implementation-critical details—such as conversion of the affine fundamental matrix to calibrated poses, joint refinement parameterization, candidate handling, and three-view inlier-score aggregation—to the released code rather than specifying them directly.

strengths: The manuscript tackles an important and notoriously difficult three-view pose problem with a practical four-correspondence solution. The reviewed source is :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/run-20260914-03/reviews/cvpr2025--gpt56_sol/review-experiment-3otft9q9/call-8ee65627d83b4fdc914e53df549b7049/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"}.

The core mean-point construction is simple, original, and useful: it converts four two-view correspondences into a five-point problem and then registers the third camera with P3P. The affine alternative and the delta-shift, early non-minimal refitting, filtering, and short LM refinement form a coherent practical system using standard solver components.

The empirical evaluation is unusually extensive for a minimal-solver paper: 90,000 triplets from 18 real scenes across PhotoTourism, Cambridge Landmarks, and Aachen; two RANSAC frameworks; per-scene results; synthetic view-angle, depth, distance, noise, and outlier studies; threshold sensitivity; and an alternative metric covering all three camera pairs.

Results support acceptance. In PoseLib, the strongest variant raises AUC@10 over 4p3v(HC) from 73.53 to 77.14 on PhotoTourism, 64.58 to 66.95 on Cambridge, and 55.20 to 57.42 on Aachen. The qualitative ranking also persists under GC-RANSAC and the alternative pose metric.

The work is reproducible in principle: code and data links are provided, the matching pipeline, RANSAC settings, delta validation, refinement count, hardware, and individual solver runtimes are documented.
weaknesses: Material: the method remains heuristic. The lemma bounds the pseudo-correspondence's epipolar deviation only by triangle extent and provides no bound on pose error or convergence. The experiments confirm sensitivity to viewpoint and scene geometry, while the raw affine solver fails badly; strong performance depends on ENM and local refinement.

Material: comparison with HC does not fully isolate the contribution. The solver-agnostic four-point LM refinement is not reported for HC even though it appears applicable to an HC initialization. Moreover, full-RANSAC HC timings include an approximately 45 ms per-run model/data-loading cost that could be amortized, whereas raw 4p3v(M±delta) is slower than HC (218.71 versus 66.06 microseconds). Thus, the speed advantage is implementation- and deployment-dependent.

The improvement over the equally enhanced 5pt+P3P baseline is modest: AUC@10 gains are 0.94, 0.64, and 0.31 points on the three benchmarks, while the most accurate variant costs roughly 1.7-2 times more runtime. The paper nevertheless establishes useful Pareto alternatives, including a faster affine-based variant.

Generality is not fully tested: all real experiments use SuperPoint/LightGlue cycle-consistent three-view tracks, and there is no analysis of camera ordering, which view pair is estimated first, or which three of the four points form the mean. Several solver-only synthetic plots also select the lowest-error solution using ground truth and are therefore optimistic, although the real RANSAC results substantially mitigate this concern.

Presentation refinements include crowded tables and many similarly named variants, occasional inconsistent '+C' versus '+F' notation, and underspecified point/view ordering. These issues affect clarity and exact reimplementation but do not undermine the central contribution.

strengths: The paper addresses a difficult and practically relevant three-view pose problem. Its central construction—creating an approximate fifth correspondence from three point means, applying the standard five-point solver, and registering the third camera with P3P—is simple, original in this context, and easy to integrate into robust estimation. :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/run-20260914-03/reviews/cvpr2025--gpt56_sol/review-experiment-r192kc0f/call-e2913e3f2b7e4fdd8032fdae86ebfd2f/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"}

The geometric lemma correctly motivates why the mean-point epipolar residual is bounded, and the algebraic discussion explains why the constructed correspondence generically supplies an additional essential-matrix equation under perspective projection.

The empirical evaluation is unusually broad: approximately 90,000 triplets from 18 scenes across PhotoTourism, Cambridge Landmarks, and Aachen; synthetic geometry and noise studies; outlier and threshold experiments; per-scene results; an alternative three-pair pose metric; and evaluations in both PoseLib and GC-RANSAC.

The paper includes strong practical baselines, notably both the prior homotopy-continuation solver and 5pt+P3P. Applying the proposed refinement, filtering, and ENM components to 5pt+P3P is especially useful for separating the benefit of four-point sampling from generic engineering improvements.

Results support practical utility. The proposed variants consistently improve accuracy-runtime curves, and in GC-RANSAC the refined mean-point methods improve AUC@10 over 5pt+P3P by roughly 2–3 points across the three benchmarks.

The manuscript is generally clear and visually polished. Public source-code and data links, stated feature pipelines, thresholds, validation protocol, runtimes, and extensive ablations make reproducibility substantially better than for the prior specialized solvers.
weaknesses: Material: the comparison with 4p3v(HC) does not isolate the solver contribution fairly. The proposed methods receive the generic per-hypothesis LM refinement (+R), but no 4p3v(HC)+R result is reported, even though HC also relaxes part of the fourth correspondence and could apparently be refined on all four original triplets. Since +R accounts for much of the reported gain—for example, in GC-RANSAC 4p3v(M) is essentially tied with HC before refinement—this omission weakens the central state-of-the-art claim.

Material: improvements over the enhanced 5pt+P3P baseline are consistent but modest relative to their cost in PoseLib. For PhotoTourism, Cambridge, and Aachen, the strongest method improves AUC@10 by only 0.94, 0.64, and 0.31 points over 5pt+P3P+R+F+ENM while taking about 1.7–2 times longer. Thus the benefit is principally a favorable accuracy-runtime frontier under selected budgets, not an unequivocal improvement at the tabulated operating point.

Material: all real experiments retain only cycle-consistent correspondences visible in all three views. This does not test the natural advantage of the competing (5,5,3) configuration, which can use two additional pairwise matches that need not be visible in the third camera. The relative practical behavior under partial visibility or separate pairwise/triple correspondence pools therefore remains uncertain.

Material: the theoretical guarantee is weak—the bound can scale with the entire image-triangle diameter and provides neither a useful pose-error bound nor a solver-success guarantee. Important sensitivities are also not characterized directly, including the choice and ordering of the three points used for the mean, camera-pair permutation, near-collinear samples, small-baseline cases, and other degeneracies. The broad empirical results mitigate this concern but do not establish the claimed near-negligible scene dependence after ENM.

The synthetic solver plots select the ground-truth-best candidate among all returned solutions. This measures whether a good hypothesis exists, which is relevant to RANSAC, but does not characterize candidate multiplicity, the fraction of usable all-inlier samples, or standalone selection reliability. Confidence intervals or paired uncertainty estimates are also absent despite several headline differences being below one AUC point.

Presentation/reproducibility refinements remain: the affine fundamental-matrix-to-pose step and the exact LM parameterization/objective are under-explained; the camera and correspondence ordering should be explicit; and there are minor inconsistencies such as duplicate/unclear table numbering, a +C versus +F typo, and wording that says a distance is “equal” where the proof establishes an upper bound. The released code reduces, but does not remove, these documentation issues.

The mean-point pseudo-correspondence is a modest but original practical idea. The shifted variants, early non-minimal refitting, fourth-point filtering, and refinement form a coherent robust-estimation pipeline rather than an isolated solver trick.

The evaluation is unusually extensive: 90,000 triplets across 18 scenes from three real datasets, two RANSAC frameworks, fixed-runtime comparisons, synthetic noise and outlier studies, threshold sensitivity, per-scene results, and an alternative pose-error definition.

The complete method has a credible empirical advantage. In PoseLib, the strongest variant obtains AUC@10 of 77.14/66.95/57.42 on PhotoTourism/Cambridge/Aachen, compared with 73.53/64.58/55.20 for HC and 76.20/66.31/57.11 for the enhanced 5pt+P3P baseline. Fixed-budget curves provide more useful support than benchmark maxima alone.
Reproducibility is supported by released code and data, reported parameter choices, a held-out scene for tuning, runtimes for both solvers and full RANSAC pipelines, and generally clear exposition.
weaknesses: The stated theoretical bound contains an error: from an epipolar line intersecting the triangle one obtains distance(mean,line) less than or equal to the maximum distance from the mean to a vertex, not equality as claimed. More importantly, this loose, triangle-size-dependent bound neither guarantees a small residual nor bounds pose error or solver success.

The basic proposed solver is not itself state of the art: 4p3v(M) trails ordinary 5pt+P3P on all three main AUC@10 results, while 4p3v(A) fails badly without ENM. Most of the advantage comes from multiple hypotheses, non-minimal refitting, filtering, and nonlinear optimization; the contribution should therefore be characterized as a practical pipeline rather than a strong standalone solution to 4p3v.

Against the comparably enhanced 5pt+P3P baseline, the best AUC@10 gains are only 0.94, 0.64, and 0.31 points, while runtimes rise from 56.52/47.07/76.86 ms to 112.60/81.98/139.19 ms. Confidence intervals or paired significance estimates are absent, making these small aggregate gains difficult to interpret.

The state-of-the-art comparison is incomplete. The method of Nister and Schaffalitzky is evaluated only in an oracle form because its supplied implementation could not be run, while the HC baseline uses a classifier trained on ETH3D without a matched-domain retraining study. These facts limit the breadth of the superiority claim.

The method is asymmetric, but the manuscript does not adequately specify or analyze the choice of the initial camera pair, which three of four tracks define the mean correspondence and P3P instance, or sensitivity to permutations and poorly conditioned subsets. Degenerate geometry and hypothesis failure rates are likewise not reported.

Using the standard all-inlier-sample formula for 0.9999-confidence early termination is not theoretically justified for an approximate solver whose conditional success probability can be well below one. The minimum-iteration safeguard and fixed-iteration experiments mitigate the empirical concern, but the stated confidence interpretation remains unsupported.

strengths: The mean-point pseudo-correspondence is a simple, original, and practically useful way to turn the difficult 4p3v problem into standard 5-point and P3P calls. The proposed variants are substantially easier to implement than the homotopy-continuation baseline.

The evaluation is unusually broad: 90,000 triplets across 18 scenes, three real-data benchmarks, synthetic geometry/noise studies, two RANSAC frameworks, threshold and outlier analyses, component ablations, fixed-iteration speed–accuracy curves, and an alternative all-camera-pairs metric.

The empirical contribution is supported. In PoseLib, 4p3v(M±δ)+R+F+ENM improves AUC@10 over 4p3v(HC) from 73.53 to 77.14 on PhotoTourism, 64.58 to 66.95 on Cambridge, and 55.20 to 57.42 on Aachen. The affine variant obtains approximately the accuracy of the enhanced 5pt+P3P baseline at markedly lower reported runtime.
Reproducibility is helped by released code and data, explicit hyperparameters, standard solver components, hardware information, and extensive supplementary experiments.
weaknesses: The advantage over the strongest enhanced 5pt+P3P baseline is modest: AUC@10 gains are only 0.94, 0.64, and 0.31 on the three datasets, while the best-accuracy M±δ configuration is roughly twice as slow at the reported early-termination operating point. No confidence intervals or per-scene statistical tests establish the reliability of these small aggregate differences.

The theoretical support is limited. The lemma only bounds the pseudo-match error by a triangle-size quantity that can be arbitrarily loose and provides no bound on pose error or solver success. Indeed, the unmodified affine solver has 36–41 degree average error on the real benchmarks, and the practical performance depends heavily on ENM and local refinement.

Several synthetic experiments select the returned solution with the lowest ground-truth pose error. This oracle selection particularly favors M±δ, which invokes the 5-point solver three times and therefore produces more candidates; these plots do not measure deployable hypothesis selection or failure rates.

Because an all-inlier four-point sample can still yield a poor approximate hypothesis, the usual RANSAC confidence calculation does not directly apply unless conditional solver-success probability is modeled. The manuscript reports 0.9999 early-termination confidence without explaining such an adjustment; fixed-iteration curves partly mitigate this concern.

The method privileges the first two cameras, and the shifted-mean construction is directional, yet sensitivity to camera permutation, pair selection, small baselines, planar/collinear degeneracies, or calibration error is not evaluated. Real tests also use only landmark datasets and triplets with at least ten cycle-consistent SuperPoint/LightGlue matches, limiting evidence for other front ends and scarce-track regimes.

Presentation and reproducibility refinements remain: the manuscript does not explain how the affine fundamental matrix is converted into a calibrated pose, precisely define the +F error across view pairs or the LM objective/parameterization, or clearly specify point ordering. Exact duplicate Cambridge rows for different methods in Table 7 also warrant verification. These are correctable and do not outweigh the supported practical contribution.

The geometric observation that the epipolar line induced by one triangle's centroid intersects the corresponding triangle gives useful intuition for the approximation. Ablations substantiate the choices of displacement, refinement iterations, ENM, and filtering.

weaknesses: The strongest state-of-the-art claim is partly confounded by optimization. Runtime accounting also deserves clarification because the supplement reports approximately 45 ms for loading HC data once per RANSAC run, an overhead that could normally be cached across runs.

The theoretical guarantee is weak: bounding the centroid's epipolar error by the triangle radius can yield an image-scale bound and provides neither a tight accuracy guarantee nor a probability that an all-inlier sample generates a usable hypothesis. The independence argument for the pseudo-correspondence is generic rather than a complete characterization of degeneracies.

All real benchmarks use landmark/localization imagery and one SuperPoint–LightGlue correspondence pipeline. strengths: The paper addresses the difficult and practically relevant four-point/three-view relative-pose problem with a simple, implementable construction using established 5-point and P3P solvers.

The mean-point pseudo-correspondence is intuitive and reasonably original. Its geometric motivation is supported by a lemma, barycentric-coordinate studies, and synthetic experiments over camera angle, scene depth, distance, noise, and outliers.

The evaluation is unusually broad: approximately 90,000 triplets from 18 scenes across PhotoTourism, Cambridge Landmarks, and Aachen, two RANSAC frameworks, per-scene results, ablations, threshold sensitivity, and an alternative error metric including all camera pairs.

Results consistently support practical usefulness. In PoseLib, the strongest method raises AUC@10 over 4p3v(HC) from 73.53 to 77.14 on PhotoTourism, 64.58 to 66.95 on Cambridge, and 55.20 to 57.42 on Aachen; GC-RANSAC experiments show similar trends.
Public code and data, named solver implementations, reported hyperparameters, hardware, and runtime measurements provide a good basis for reproduction.
weaknesses: Materially, the comparison to 4p3v(HC) is not fully controlled. The proposed methods receive per-hypothesis refinement using the unused constraint of the fourth three-view point, whereas no HC+R counterpart is reported even though the relaxed HC solution appears amenable to the same full-(4,4,4) refinement. This matters because the unrefined 4p3v(M) is slightly less accurate than HC, and much of the gain comes from +R.

The practical comparison with 5pt+P3P restricts inputs to matches consistent across all three views. That baseline intrinsically needs only three common tracks and may take its other two correspondences from the first image pair, while the proposed method requires four common tracks. Evaluation with partial visibility is therefore needed to establish the claimed practical advantage in the baseline's natural operating regime.

The accuracy gains over the enhanced 5pt+P3P baseline in PoseLib are modest—under one AUC@10 point on all three datasets—and no uncertainty estimates are reported. The most accurate proposed variant is also substantially slower in the early-termination tables. Runtime conclusions are further affected by loading HC data once per RANSAC, a reported approximately 45 ms overhead that could be amortized in a persistent deployment.

The theoretical guarantee is weak: bounding the pseudo-match error by the triangle radius can be arbitrarily loose and does not characterize pose error or failure configurations. The supplementary statement that the maximum distance to an intersecting epipolar line is “equal” to the maximum distance to a triangle vertex should instead be an inequality. The axis-aligned ±δ construction remains primarily heuristic.

Several implementation-critical details are insufficiently specified in the manuscript, including conversion of the affine fundamental matrix into a Euclidean pose, root and cheirality handling, and the precise parameterization and residuals used by the inner LM refinement. Released code mitigates this reproducibility concern, but the paper is not fully self-contained.

Reviewed source: :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/run-20260914-03/reviews/cvpr2025--gpt56_sol/review-experiment-0umdi6kr/call-bce14ce601234b228fbdd2a2edce1215/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"}
weaknesses: The improvement over the strongest enhanced 5pt+P3P baseline is modest and comes at appreciable cost: the best PoseLib variant improves AUC@10 by only 0.94/0.64/0.31 points while taking 112.60/81.98/139.19 ms rather than 56.52/47.07/76.86 ms. Paired confidence intervals or significance estimates are absent, making these small aggregate differences difficult to interpret.

The theory justifies an approximate image constraint, not pose accuracy or optimizer convergence. Its bound is loose and scales with the triangle extent. Empirically, the unmodified affine solver fails badly and the mean-based solver often needs ENM and local refinement to become competitive, so the contribution is primarily a robust-estimation pipeline rather than a reliably accurate standalone solver.

The construction is asymmetric: views 1 and 2 estimate geometry and view 3 is registered afterward. The paper does not study sensitivity to camera ordering or offer a pair-selection rule, nor does it isolate difficult cases such as very low parallax, near-planar geometry, severe calibration error, or elongated triangles.

The state-of-the-art comparison is not fully conclusive. The Nistér–Schaffalitzky method is evaluated only in an oracle form because its code could not be run; the HC anchor count and retraining/tuning choices are insufficiently detailed; and the GC-RANSAC comparison omits the generic +R/+F-enhanced 5pt+P3P baseline that is shown to matter in PoseLib.

Several core implementation details are not self-contained, notably how the affine fundamental matrix is converted into a calibrated metric pose for triangulation, the exact refinement parameterization and residual, three-view inlier aggregation, and multiple-solution selection. Public code mitigates this reproducibility concern but does not replace a precise algorithm specification.

Presentation issues are secondary but noticeable: the many variants are difficult to track, Tables 2 and 3 are substantially redundant, +C appears where +F is intended, and the text occasionally states equality where only an upper-bound relationship was established.

strengths: The paper offers a simple but useful practical contribution for the difficult 4p3v problem: it converts four three-view correspondences into hypotheses using established 4-point affine/5-point/P3P components, avoiding the complexity and high failure rate of prior homotopy- or epipole-sampling-based approaches.

The empirical study is unusually broad for a geometric solver paper: 90,000 triplets from 18 scenes across PhotoTourism, Cambridge Landmarks, and Aachen, supplemented by controlled studies of image noise, view angle, scene depth, outlier ratio, and RANSAC threshold sensitivity.

The strongest method consistently improves accuracy over both 4p3v(HC) and the enhanced 5pt+P3P baseline. For example, PoseLib AUC@10 improves from 76.20/66.31/57.11 for 5pt+P3P+R+F+ENM to 77.14/66.95/57.42 on PhotoTourism/Cambridge/Aachen. Fixed-budget curves further support a favorable speed–accuracy trade-off.

The experiments carefully ablate the mean-point perturbation, fourth-point refinement, filtering, and early non-minimal refitting. Parameters are selected on a held-out scene, results are reported per scene and in two RANSAC frameworks, and an alternative metric including all three camera pairs preserves the ranking.

The method is relevant to robust multiview estimation, technically plausible, and comparatively easy to implement. Reported source code and data, together with specified matching, thresholds, iteration counts, and solver components, support reproducibility.
weaknesses: Material: the advantage over the strongest enhanced 5pt+P3P baseline is modest—generally below one AUC@10 point—and no paired confidence intervals or run-to-run variability are reported. This matters because the most accurate M±δ variant is also substantially slower under early termination, e.g. 112.60 versus 56.52 ms on PhotoTourism and 139.19 versus 76.86 ms on Aachen.

Material: the useful result is primarily a refined RANSAC pipeline rather than an accurate standalone 4p3v estimator. Raw 4p3v(M) is usually weaker than 5pt+P3P, raw 4p3v(A) fails badly in PoseLib, and most gains require fourth-point LM refinement and/or ENM. Applicability may therefore depend on the availability and behavior of these local-optimization stages.

Material: the theoretical support for the mean-point heuristic is limited. The triangle-based epipolar-error bound can be very loose and does not guarantee a pose within the optimizer's convergence basin; moreover, the text states an equality where the geometric argument establishes only an upper bound. The cross-term argument for independence of the synthetic constraint is also more an intuition than a complete generic-rank proof.

Material: all real-data tests use the same SuperPoint–LightGlue correspondence pipeline and select triplets having at least ten three-view matches and 10% overlap. The outlier study uses uniformly random synthetic outliers and stops at 40% inliers, leaving performance under structured mismatches, lower-overlap cases, alternative feature pipelines, and important near-degenerate motions less established.

Presentation: the many solver suffixes and extremely dense result tables make the paper harder to parse, and concise pseudocode specifying hypothesis enumeration, cheirality handling, inlier scoring, and ENM sampling would improve self-contained reproducibility. These are refinements rather than reasons for rejection.

strengths: The paper addresses the difficult and practically relevant 4p3v calibrated relative-pose problem with an appealingly simple approach: approximate the first two-view geometry, then reuse mature 5-point and P3P solvers.

The mean-point construction is original and technically motivated. The supplementary lemma bounds its epipolar discrepancy using the projected triangle, and the manuscript explains why it provides a generically additional constraint for perspective cameras.

The empirical study is unusually broad: approximately 90,000 triplets from 18 scenes across three datasets, two RANSAC frameworks, synthetic noise/view-angle/depth experiments, threshold and inlier-ratio sensitivity tests, and ablations of refinement, filtering, and ENM.

The reported results substantiate practical usefulness. For example, the full mean-point variant obtains AUC@10 values of 77.14, 66.95, and 57.42 on PhotoTourism, Cambridge, and Aachen, respectively, versus 73.53, 64.58, and 55.20 for the prior HC solver. Faster proposed variants also provide competitive speed-accuracy trade-offs.

Reproducibility is strong overall: source code and data are linked, and the manuscript specifies solvers, feature pipeline, RANSAC settings, thresholds, refinement count, shift parameter, and timing hardware.
weaknesses: The core solver is approximate and offers no bound on final pose error or refinement convergence; the geometric lemma only gives a potentially loose bound on the synthetic correspondence. Practical success depends substantially on ENM, local optimization, and filtering, while the unrefined affine variant fails badly in PoseLib.

Accuracy gains over the strengthened 5pt+P3P baseline are modest relative to the cost of the most accurate variant. Its runtimes are 112.60 versus 56.52 ms, 81.98 versus 47.07 ms, and 139.19 versus 76.86 ms on the three dataset aggregates, so the efficiency claim applies mainly to selected lighter variants rather than the best-accuracy configuration.

The main evaluation metric omits the 2-3 pose and therefore does not assess the distinctive relative-baseline-scale component of three-view pose. The supplementary metric including the 2-3 translation direction preserves the ranking, which mitigates this concern, but direct relative-scale or reconstruction-error evaluation remains absent.
No confidence intervals, repeated-seed variation, or significance analysis is reported. This matters because several improvements over the refined 5-point baseline are only about 0.3-1.0 AUC points.

Failure regimes are not characterized systematically, particularly low parallax and degenerate or nearly collinear point configurations. The experiments cover several useful factors, but the acknowledged scene dependence and reliance on refinement limit the generality of the conclusions.

Comparison with the earlier solver of Nister and Schaffalitzky is restricted to an oracle experiment because its full implementation could not be run. In addition, Table 7 contains exactly duplicated Cambridge rows for distinct affine- and mean-based configurations, suggesting a reporting error that weakens confidence in that secondary evaluation.

strengths: The paper addresses an important and notoriously difficult three-view relative-pose problem with a refreshingly simple construction based on established 5-point and P3P solvers. The approach is practical and substantially easier to implement than the homotopy-continuation baseline. Reviewed source: :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/run-20260914-03/reviews/cvpr2025--gpt56_sol/review-experiment-nmixi3uf/call-f76ae1441ee2495f80adb2df95c08695/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"}.

The empirical evaluation is unusually extensive for a geometric solver: approximately 90,000 triplets from 18 scenes across PhotoTourism, Cambridge Landmarks, and Aachen; two RANSAC frameworks; fixed-iteration speed-accuracy curves; and experiments varying noise, outlier ratio, threshold, scene geometry, and camera geometry.

The strongest mean-point variant consistently improves end-to-end PoseLib accuracy. Its AUC@10 is 77.14/66.95/57.42 on the three dataset groups, versus 73.53/64.58/55.20 for 4p3v(HC) and 76.20/66.31/57.11 for the enhanced 5pt+P3P baseline. GC-RANSAC experiments and an alternative all-pairs pose metric broadly preserve the ranking.
The ablations separately study the mean-point displacement, two-step LM refinement, filtering, and early non-minimal refitting. Per-scene plots reveal rather than conceal scene-dependent behavior.

The geometric lemma gives useful intuition for why the synthetic mean correspondence is not arbitrary, while public code and data, named solver implementations, thresholds, feature pipeline, and runtime hardware provide a reasonably strong reproducibility basis.
weaknesses: Material: the proposed estimator is a heuristic approximation, not a solution of the exact 4p3v equations. The lemma only implies that the pseudo-correspondence's epipolar line intersects a projected triangle, yielding a potentially very loose image-space bound proportional to triangle size. It provides no perturbation bound on the recovered pose, conditioning analysis, or probability that an all-inlier sample generates a useful hypothesis.

Material: the state-of-the-art result is not cleanly attributable to the mean-point construction. Without the additional machinery, 4p3v(M) has AUC@10 of 72.56/64.06/55.06, generally below both 5pt+P3P and 4p3v(HC). The strongest results rely on generic per-hypothesis LM refinement, filtering, and ENM. Although the paper strengthens 5pt+P3P similarly, it does not report an HC baseline followed by the same generic four-point LM refinement, leaving an important fairness question.

Material: improvements over the strengthened 5pt+P3P baseline are modest—0.94, 0.64, and 0.31 AUC@10—while the best variant takes roughly 112.6/82.0/139.2 ms versus 56.5/47.1/76.9 ms. Speed-accuracy curves help, but confidence intervals, repeated-seed variability, or significance analysis are absent, so the robustness of these small margins is unclear.

Material: the solver is asymmetric, yet the manuscript does not study sensitivity to which camera pair is processed first or clearly specify how the three points used for the mean correspondence and P3P are selected from the four-point sample. This matters because the paper itself shows strong dependence on view angle and geometry.

The evaluation uses only fully cycle-consistent SuperPoint/LightGlue tracks and nominally calibrated landmark datasets. Results under calibration error, alternative matching pipelines, and direct relative-scale error would better establish practical generality; this limits, but does not invalidate, the demonstrated contribution.

Presentation/minor: after Lemma 1, the manuscript says the distance to the epipolar line is “equal” to the maximum distance to a triangle vertex; the proved statement is an upper-bound inequality. Several implementation details—normalization, precise three-view scoring, ENM thresholds, and sample ordering—should also be stated explicitly even if available in code.

strengths: The paper tackles an important, notoriously difficult multiview-geometry problem with a clever and practical idea: constructing an approximate mean-point correspondence reduces 4p3v estimation to mature 5-point and P3P components. This is simple to implement and potentially useful in robust estimation pipelines.

The technical motivation is sound. The supplement explains why the mean-point constraint is generally independent for a perspective essential matrix and proves that its epipolar line intersects the corresponding image triangle.

The evaluation is unusually extensive: 90,000 triplets across 18 scenes and three real datasets, two RANSAC frameworks, per-scene results, an alternative all-camera-pairs metric, and synthetic studies of noise, viewing angle, scene depth, camera distance, outlier ratio, threshold sensitivity, and hyperparameters.

The results support practical value. In PoseLib, 4p3v(M)+R+F exceeds 4p3v(HC) in AUC@10 on PhotoTourism, Cambridge, and Aachen (75.14/65.71/56.28 versus 73.53/64.58/55.20) while also running faster. GC-RANSAC broadly confirms the ranking, and different variants offer useful speed-accuracy trade-offs.

Reproducibility is strong overall: source code and data are publicly identified, important settings such as the delta scale and LM iteration count are reported, validation uses a held-out scene, and the exposition clearly distinguishes the approximate kernel from its refinements.
weaknesses: The main state-of-the-art comparison is not fully controlled. The proposed methods receive generic sample-level LM refinement using the fourth triplet (+R), which the ablations identify as a major source of improvement, but no analogous 4p3v(HC)+R result is reported. This weakens attribution of the gains specifically to the proposed hypothesis construction.

The theoretical guarantee is limited: triangle intersection only yields a potentially loose image-space bound dependent on triangle size, with no bound on pose error or probability of producing a usable hypothesis. Indeed, the noise-free experiments show nonzero and sometimes substantial raw-solver error, so practical performance relies heavily on ENM, LM refinement, and RANSAC local optimization.

Against the strongest enhanced 5pt+P3P baseline, the most accurate variant provides modest AUC@10 gains of 0.94, 0.64, and 0.31 points across the three datasets while requiring roughly 1.7–2 times the runtime. Confidence intervals or paired significance analyses are absent, making these small accuracy differences difficult to interpret.

All real-data correspondences come from one SuperPoint-LightGlue pipeline and are required to be consistent across all three views. Consequently, the experiments do not test different matchers or the partial-visibility regime motivating the contrast with the (5,5,3) baseline; low-inlier robustness is examined semi-synthetically on only one scene.

Some implementation details are deferred to code, including sample ordering, selection among multiple 5-point/P3P solutions, and the precise refinement residuals. Table 7 also contains exactly duplicated Cambridge results for distinct affine- and mean-based variants, suggesting a reporting error that should be verified. These are reproducibility/presentation concerns rather than rejection-level defects.

strengths: The paper addresses a difficult and practically relevant calibrated three-view pose problem. The reviewed source includes the complete manuscript and supplement: :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/run-20260914-03/reviews/cvpr2025--gpt56_sol/review-experiment-e8aurfk1/call-0472a66a483c43d2a9993b00d3b198a9/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"}.

The mean-point pseudo-correspondence is a simple but original way to turn four two-view matches into input for established 5-point and P3P solvers. The resulting methods are practical, modular, and substantially easier to implement than the homotopy-continuation baseline.

The empirical study is unusually broad for a geometric-solver paper: 90,000 triplets spanning 18 scenes from PhotoTourism, Cambridge Landmarks, and Aachen, evaluations in both PoseLib and GC-RANSAC, per-scene curves, threshold and outlier analyses, synthetic tests, and component ablations.

The proposed methods demonstrate useful speed-accuracy trade-offs rather than merely isolated best numbers. For example, in PoseLib, 4p3v(M)+R+F improves AUC@10 over 4p3v(HC) on PhotoTourism, Cambridge, and Aachen (75.14/65.71/56.28 versus 73.53/64.58/55.20) while also reducing runtime (30.88/22.72/42.38 ms versus 64.10/60.11/67.26 ms).

The supplement checks an alternative metric involving all three camera pairs and finds the ranking unchanged. Public code and data links, disclosed hardware, parameter ablations, and an explicit limitations discussion further support reproducibility.
weaknesses: The theoretical justification is considerably weaker than the empirical evidence. The lemma only bounds the pseudo-match epipolar error by a triangle-scale quantity that can itself be arbitrarily large and gives no bound on recovered pose error or solver success. The subsequent statement that the distance is “equal” to the maximum distance from the mean to the vertices is not established for the particular epipolar line; the proof supports an inequality. Required visibility/nondegeneracy assumptions should also be explicit.

Important implementation details are not self-contained: the manuscript does not clearly specify how the affine fundamental matrix is converted into calibrated camera poses, how cheirality and multiple 5-point/P3P solutions are handled, the parameterization and residual used by three-view LM refinement, or exactly how pairwise errors are combined for triplet inlier scoring. Released code mitigates but does not remove this reproducibility concern.

The accuracy advantage over the fully enhanced 5pt+P3P baseline is modest and lacks uncertainty estimates. In PoseLib, the strongest 4p3v(M±δ)+R+F+ENM variant improves AUC@10 by only 0.94, 0.64, and 0.31 points across the three datasets while taking roughly 1.7–2 times longer. The paper supports a favorable Pareto trade-off, but claims of clear accuracy superiority should be tempered.

The GC-RANSAC comparison is not fully controlled: proposed methods receive the influential +R refinement, whereas 5pt+P3P+R(+F) is omitted even though the manuscript states these operations are applicable and the evaluated tracks are visible in all three views. The PoseLib experiment contains this stronger baseline and shows much narrower gaps, so the second-framework superiority claim is not fully substantiated.

Several synthetic plots select, using ground truth, the lowest-error solution from each solver's returned hypotheses. This measures oracle solution-set coverage rather than deployable estimation and can favor 4p3v(M±δ), which invokes the 5-point solver three times and returns more candidates.

Evaluation excludes low-overlap triplets and requires at least ten consistently matched three-view tracks. Degenerate or adverse cases such as tiny/collinear image triangles, near-planar scenes, low parallax, and near-pure rotation are not isolated. Moreover, standard RANSAC early-termination confidence is not formally valid for an approximate minimal solver whose all-inlier samples can still fail; fixed-iteration curves partly alleviate this concern.

Presentation refinements are needed but are not acceptance-determining: the many A/M/δ/R/F/ENM variants make tables difficult to parse, some figures are visually dense, and several typographical errors remain.

strengths: The paper addresses the difficult and practically relevant four-point, three-calibrated-view relative-pose problem. The mean-point construction is simple, apparently original in this setting, and turns existing efficient 5-point and P3P implementations into a usable approximate solver.

The empirical evaluation is unusually broad: 90,000 camera triplets from 18 scenes across PhotoTourism, Cambridge Landmarks, and Aachen, using both PoseLib and GC-RANSAC. It also includes fixed-iteration speed–accuracy curves, individual-scene results, noise and outlier studies, threshold sensitivity, ablations, and an alternative metric covering all three camera pairs.

Comparisons include both the specialized homotopy-continuation method and the strong 5pt+P3P baseline. Importantly, the authors also equip 5pt+P3P with their refinement, filtering, and early-refitting strategies, making the main comparison more informative.

The reduced sample size produces a credible practical advantage in contaminated data. The semi-synthetic 40% inlier experiment shows a substantial speed–accuracy benefit, and the proposed variants generally outperform the prior 4p3v(HC) method across datasets and RANSAC frameworks.
Reproducibility is helped substantially by released source code, archived data, reported parameters, hardware, feature pipeline, and numerous supplementary ablations.
weaknesses: The advantage over the strongest enhanced 5pt+P3P baseline is modest in the principal PoseLib table and costs appreciable runtime. AUC@10 gains are only 0.94, 0.64, and 0.31 points on the three benchmarks, while runtimes rise from 56.52 to 112.60 ms, 47.07 to 81.98 ms, and 76.86 to 139.19 ms. No confidence intervals or run-to-run variability are reported for these small differences.

Most of the final performance comes from standard downstream machinery rather than the raw approximation. Unmodified 4p3v(M) is worse than 5pt+P3P on all three PoseLib benchmarks, and unmodified 4p3v(A) fails badly there, with average errors of roughly 36–41 degrees. The contribution is therefore best understood as an effective initialization-and-refinement pipeline, not a generally accurate four-point solver by itself.

The theoretical guarantee is weak and contains a mathematical misstatement. Line–triangle intersection implies d(m2, Em1) is at most the maximum distance from m2 to a triangle vertex; the supplement incorrectly says these quantities are equal. Moreover, this scale-dependent image-space bound can be very loose and provides no bound on pose error or probability of successful refinement.

Several details needed for a self-contained reproduction are underspecified: which three of the four points define the mean and P3P instance, coordinate normalization, affine-matrix-to-pose conversion, enumeration and cheirality filtering of 5-point/P3P solutions, the exact three-view LM parameterization and residual, and the two-view ENM procedure. Public code mitigates but does not remove this clarity issue.

The synthetic solver experiments select, using ground truth, the returned solution with the lowest pose error. This oracle protocol especially favors 4p3v(M±δ), which invokes the 5-point solver three times and returns more hypotheses; those plots therefore do not measure deployable standalone accuracy. The real RANSAC experiments are more persuasive.

A direct practical comparison with the earlier method of Nistér and Schaffalitzky is absent because neither group could run its epipole-sampling code; only an oracle version is discussed. Crowded plots, duplicated main-result tables, an unexplained color encoding, and minor notation/label errors are presentation refinements rather than rejection-level defects. Overall, the supported practical contribution outweighs these reservations, but the modest gains and limited theory favor weak accept rather than full accept.

strengths: The mean-point pseudo-correspondence is a simple, original, and practical way to obtain four-correspondence hypotheses using established 5-point and P3P solvers. The ±δ variant and use of the fourth third-view observation are sensible extensions.

The empirical evaluation is unusually broad for a geometric solver paper: 90,000 triplets from 18 scenes across PhotoTourism, Cambridge Landmarks, and Aachen; two RANSAC frameworks; and studies of noise, outlier ratio, viewpoint, scene depth, thresholds, and an alternative pose metric.

The reported gains are consistent across datasets. In PoseLib, 4p3v(M±δ)+R+F+ENM improves AUC@10 over enhanced 5pt+P3P from 76.20 to 77.14, 66.31 to 66.95, and 57.11 to 57.42 on the three benchmarks, respectively; the affine variant provides a faster competitive operating point. GC-RANSAC results also favor the proposed refined solvers.
Ablations support the importance of refinement, ENM, δ, and filtering, while parameter choices are validated on a scene excluded from the main aggregate evaluation.
Reproducibility is strong overall: archived code and data are provided, and the paper reports matcher settings, thresholds, iteration schedules, hardware, δ, and the number of LM steps.
weaknesses: The theoretical support is limited. Lemma 1 only yields a loose image-space bound proportional to the triangle size and provides no bound on essential-matrix or pose error. Moreover, the text incorrectly states that the point-to-line distance is equal to the maximum distance to the triangle vertices; only an upper-bound inequality follows.

The best PoseLib accuracy gains over the enhanced 5pt+P3P baseline are modest—0.31 to 0.94 AUC@10 points—while its runtimes rise from 56.52/47.07/76.86 ms to 112.60/81.98/139.19 ms. Speed-accuracy curves partly address this trade-off, but no uncertainty or repeated-run statistics are reported for the small margins.

Several synthetic experiments select, using ground truth, the lowest-error solution among all hypotheses. This oracle protocol is not deployable and favors variants such as M±δ that produce more candidates; those plots therefore measure candidate-set coverage rather than practical selection accuracy. The real RANSAC experiments mitigate, but do not remove, this interpretive limitation.

Important implementation details are underspecified in the manuscript, including conversion of the affine fundamental matrix into a calibrated pose, cheirality/hypothesis handling, and the exact LM parameterization and residual. It is also unclear whether the enhanced 5pt+P3P baseline uses both additional third-view observations available in the cycle-consistent evaluation data, which matters given the narrow margins.

Generalization evidence is restricted to one feature/matcher pipeline and mostly landmark imagery. The outlier stress test uses independently generated random points, leaving structured mismatches, low-parallax cases, and explicit degeneracies insufficiently characterized.

There are correctable reporting issues: the text twice refers to a nonexistent “+C” modification instead of “+F,” and Table 7 contains Cambridge rows for M+R+F variants that exactly duplicate the corresponding affine rows across all metrics and runtime, suggesting a copy or tabulation error.

strengths: The paper addresses an important and difficult three-view pose problem with a simple, original construction: four real correspondences plus a mean-point pseudo-correspondence enable reuse of efficient 5-point and P3P solvers. The resulting implementation is substantially simpler than prior homotopy- or curve-sampling-based approaches.

The practical pipeline is thoughtfully designed. Early non-minimal refitting limits error propagation, while filtering and joint refinement exploit the otherwise-unused fourth observation in the third view. The argument that the mean-point constraint is generically additional under perspective projection is plausible.

The evaluation is unusually extensive: approximately 90,000 real image triplets spanning PhotoTourism, Cambridge Landmarks, and Aachen; two RANSAC frameworks; synthetic studies of viewpoint, depth, noise, and outliers; per-scene results; threshold sensitivity; ablations; and an alternative pose metric covering all camera pairs.

The empirical improvements are consistent. In PoseLib, the strongest method raises AUC@10 from 73.53/64.58/55.20 for 4p3v(HC) to 77.14/66.95/57.42 on the three datasets, and it also improves over the strengthened 5pt+P3P pipeline. Fixed-budget plots provide useful evidence about the speed-accuracy trade-off.

Reproducibility is comparatively strong: source-code and data links are provided, and the manuscript reports matcher settings, RANSAC protocols, hardware, the delta rule, and the number of refinement iterations.
weaknesses: The method is a heuristic approximate solver rather than a consistent solution of the 4p3v equations. Its theoretical bound is only the distance from the triangle centroid to its farthest vertex, which can be image-scale and therefore does not guarantee an accurate pose. The text should also state the realized-line result as an inequality; equality applies only to the worst case over intersecting lines. Raw 4p3v(A) results are very poor, and much of the practical success depends on ENM and local optimization.

The comparison to 4p3v(HC) is not fully controlled. The proposed methods receive per-hypothesis refinement using the complete fourth correspondence, and the ablation identifies this refinement as particularly important, but no 4p3v(HC)+R result is reported even though analogous refinement appears applicable to an HC pose. Comparison with the other principal prior method, [37], is limited to an oracle-epipole variant because its full code could not be run.

Accuracy gains over the strongest 5pt+P3P baseline are modest relative to added cost. For example, the best PoseLib variant improves AUC@10 by only 0.94, 0.64, and 0.31 points over 5pt+P3P+R+F+ENM while taking roughly 1.7-2 times as long. The fixed-runtime curves support usefulness, but claims of broad practical superiority should be qualified.

Several implementation-critical details are left to the released code: the precise joint-refinement residual and pose parameterization, conversion of the affine fundamental matrix into calibrated poses, cheirality/root selection, choice of the three-point subset, and ENM inlier handling. This weakens the manuscript's self-contained reproducibility.

Synthetic solver accuracy selects the hypothesis with the lowest ground-truth error. Because the methods return different numbers of roots—and 4p3v(M±delta) deliberately generates three sets—this oracle selection can favor methods producing more hypotheses. The primary RANSAC evaluation mitigates this concern, but synthetic comparisons should additionally report success rates under an implementable selection rule. Minor reporting issues, including apparently duplicated Cambridge rows in Table 7, also merit verification.
