strengths: The paper addresses a difficult, practically relevant three-view geometry problem. Constructing an approximate fifth correspondence from three point means is simple, original in this context, and enables reuse of mature 5-point and P3P solvers.

The evaluation is unusually extensive: 90,000 triplets from 18 real-world scenes across PhotoTourism, Cambridge Landmarks, and Aachen, plus synthetic noise, outlier, camera-angle, distance, and scene-depth studies.

The strongest method consistently improves accuracy. In PoseLib, 4p3v(M±δ)+R+F+ENM raises AUC@10 over the strongest enhanced 5pt+P3P baseline from 76.20 to 77.14 on PhotoTourism, 66.31 to 66.95 on Cambridge, and 57.11 to 57.42 on Aachen; larger gains over the HC solver and consistent GC-RANSAC results strengthen the evidence.

Ablations separately examine the mean-point location, δ, refinement iterations, ENM, filtering, RANSAC thresholds, and per-scene behavior. Reporting an alternative metric covering all camera pairs also addresses a potential weakness of the primary pose metric.

Code and archived data are provided, and the method is documented well enough to understand its overall pipeline. :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/run-20260914-03/reviews/cvpr2025--gpt56_sol/review-experiment-tpmovu5n/call-52b4a6548c884aa8a50802970edce77c/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"}
weaknesses: The theoretical support is limited. The triangle-intersection lemma gives only a loose, triangle-size-dependent bound on the pseudo-correspondence's epipolar error; it does not bound pose error or characterize when the five-point system will yield a useful real solution. The ±δ construction remains empirical.

The advantage over the strongest conventional baseline is modest relative to cost. The PoseLib AUC@10 gains over enhanced 5pt+P3P are 0.94, 0.64, and 0.31 points, while runtimes rise from 56.52 to 112.60 ms, 47.07 to 81.98 ms, and 76.86 to 139.19 ms. Confidence intervals or scene-level statistical tests are absent, so the practical superiority should be stated more carefully.

Much of the final gain comes from ENM, fourth-point refinement, filtering, and local optimization rather than the raw approximate solver. The unmodified affine variant fails badly in PoseLib, while the unmodified mean-point variant is generally comparable to or weaker than 5pt+P3P. Thus, the contribution is best viewed as a complete robust-estimation design rather than a uniformly accurate standalone solver.

Evaluation uses only SuperPoint-LightGlue correspondences that form complete three-view tracks. Generalization across feature pipelines, partial-visibility patterns, and difficult degeneracies such as very small triangles, near-pure rotation, low parallax, or strongly planar configurations is not established; solver failure and real-solution statistics are also missing.

Several details are left mainly to the released code: which three of the four points define the mean and whether permutations are considered, conversion of the affine fundamental matrix to a valid pose, the exact LM residual and parameterization, and three-view scoring. It is also unclear whether HC's reported end-to-end runtime includes its stated 45 ms loading cost and whether enhanced 5pt+P3P uses both extra third-view observations; these affect comparison reproducibility.

Presentation-only issues include dense tables and plots, an unexplained near-duplication of Tables 2 and 3, inconsistent +C/+F notation, and several typographical errors. These do not materially weaken the scientific case.

strengths: The paper addresses an important and notoriously difficult geometric-estimation problem. Reducing the RANSAC sample from five correspondences to four has clear practical value for three-view reconstruction and localization.

The mean-point pseudo-correspondence is a simple, original, and useful idea. Building the resulting solvers from established 5-point and P3P components makes them substantially easier to implement than the homotopy-continuation baseline; the ENM, filtering, and short refinement stages are sensible practical additions.

The empirical evaluation is unusually broad for a minimal-solver paper: 90,000 triplets from 18 real scenes across PhotoTourism, Cambridge Landmarks, and Aachen; two RANSAC frameworks; per-scene results; alternative pose metrics; threshold, noise, outlier, scene-depth, viewing-angle, and component ablations.

The proposed methods consistently improve over 4p3v(HC). In PoseLib, the strongest variant obtains AUC@10 of 77.14 versus 73.53 on PhotoTourism, 66.95 versus 64.58 on Cambridge, and 57.42 versus 55.20 on Aachen. Results in GC-RANSAC and under the all-camera-pair error metric support the same overall conclusion.

Reproducibility is strong overall: source code and evaluation data are linked, and the manuscript reports matcher settings, validation choices, RANSAC thresholds and iteration schedules, CPU information, and solver-level and end-to-end runtimes.
weaknesses: Material concern: the advantage over the properly enhanced 5pt+P3P baseline is modest. For the strongest variants, AUC@10 improves by only 0.94, 0.64, and 0.31 points on the three datasets, without uncertainty estimates, while early-termination runtimes rise from 56.52/47.07/76.86 ms to 112.60/81.98/139.19 ms. The speed-accuracy curves are favorable, but the practical superiority is therefore more nuanced than some statements suggest.

The theoretical support is limited. Lemma 1 gives only a loose, triangle-size-dependent bound on one directed point-to-epipolar-line error, not on symmetric epipolar or pose error. Moreover, the supplement states that the distance is “equal to” the maximum centroid-to-vertex distance, whereas the proof only establishes an upper bound. This imprecision does not invalidate the empirical method but weakens its theoretical justification.

The method is asymmetric in its choice of the first two cameras, the three points used to form the mean, and the image in which the ±δ shifts are applied. View-order and three-of-four subset sensitivity are not evaluated, despite the demonstrated degradation with increasing viewing angle and the acknowledged scene dependence. This is the most important missing robustness analysis.

Several synthetic experiments select, using ground truth, the lowest-error solution among all candidates. This particularly favors 4p3v(M±δ), which invokes the 5-point solver three times and produces more candidates. These plots consequently characterize oracle recall rather than deployable stand-alone accuracy; the extensive RANSAC experiments mitigate but do not remove this interpretive limitation.

Comparison with dedicated 4p3v methods is effectively limited to 4p3v(HC); the older method of Nistér and Schaffalitzky is evaluated only with an oracle epipole because neither party could run its sampler. This is understandable, but it narrows the evidence behind the broad state-of-the-art claim.

Presentation/reproducibility refinement: the text does not fully specify how the affine fundamental matrix is converted into a valid calibrated relative pose, how camera/point ordering is chosen, or all cheirality and candidate-selection details. The released code likely resolves these questions, but the central algorithm should be reproducible from the manuscript itself. Minor notation and labeling errors, such as “+C” where “+F” is intended, should also be corrected.

strengths: The paper offers a simple and practically useful approach to a difficult three-view relative-pose problem. Constructing an approximate fifth correspondence from three mean points is original, easy to implement using standard 5-point and P3P solvers, and substantially simpler than the homotopy-continuation baseline.

The empirical evaluation is unusually broad: 90,000 triplets from 18 scenes across PhotoTourism, Cambridge Landmarks, and Aachen, complemented by synthetic studies of noise, viewpoint, scene depth, and outlier ratios.

The conclusions are supported across two robust-estimation frameworks, PoseLib and GC-RANSAC. The paper also evaluates fixed-iteration speed-accuracy curves, several RANSAC thresholds, individual scenes, and an alternative metric covering all three camera pairs.

The ablations isolate the effects of the mean-point offsets, early non-minimal refitting, fourth-point filtering, and refinement. The results consistently identify refinement as important and show that the selected offset and iteration count are not highly sensitive.

The strongest configurations improve accuracy over both 4p3v(HC) and 5pt+P3P. For example, under PoseLib, 4p3v(M±δ)+R+F+ENM obtains the highest AUC@10 on all three dataset groups, while lighter variants provide useful runtime-accuracy trade-offs.
Public code and data links, named solver implementations, reported thresholds, feature pipeline, hardware, and validation protocol provide a good basis for reproducibility.
weaknesses: The runtime comparison against 4p3v(HC) is not fully fair. The paper reports that loading its network data takes about 45 ms and charges this once per RANSAC invocation. In a normal batched or persistent application this cost would be amortized. Subtracting it would remove much of the claimed runtime dominance, and Table 5 in fact shows the loaded HC solver itself is faster than 4p3v(M). Accuracy improvements remain supported, but simultaneous accuracy-and-runtime superiority is not conclusively established.

The theoretical support for the mean-point approximation is limited. Lemma 1 only bounds epipolar distance by a quantity proportional to the triangle size, which can be arbitrarily loose and gives no bound on pose error or probability of producing a useful hypothesis. Thus the constructed correspondence remains a heuristic whose success is established mainly empirically.

The accurate variants depend heavily on non-minimal refitting and local optimization. The unmodified affine solver fails severely in PoseLib, and the basic mean solver is often comparable to rather than better than 5pt+P3P. The contribution should therefore be understood as a practical RANSAC pipeline, not an accurate direct solution of the 4p3v equations.

Several consequential choices are asymmetric but not studied: which three of the four points define the mean, which camera pair is solved first, the ordering of the two images, and the axis-aligned direction of the ±δ offsets. Permutation sensitivity and degenerate configurations are particularly relevant for a general three-view solver.

Comparison with the older solver of Nistér and Schaffalitzky is restricted to an oracle experiment because neither party could run the complete implementation. This is understandable, but it leaves the broad state-of-the-art claim only partially verified.

Some implementation-critical details are left to the released code, including conversion of the affine fundamental matrix into calibrated camera poses, branch and cheirality handling, the exact three-view scoring rule, and the LM residual and parameterization. Confidence intervals or repeated-seed variability are also absent despite several reported improvements being below one AUC point.

strengths: The centroid-based pseudo-correspondence is a simple, original, and practically useful way to turn the difficult 4p3v problem into calls to mature 5-point and P3P solvers. :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/run-20260914-03/reviews/cvpr2025--gpt56_sol/review-experiment-osxm86ug/call-34b25c8a44d94c709d2c701a214460be/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"}

The empirical evaluation is unusually extensive: 90,000 real camera triplets from 18 scenes across three datasets, two RANSAC frameworks, and additional studies of noise, outliers, camera geometry, thresholds, runtime, and an alternative three-pair pose metric.

Results consistently support practical value. For example, the strongest mean-point variant reaches PoseLib AUC@10 values of 77.14, 66.95, and 57.42 on PhotoTourism, Cambridge, and Aachen, respectively, versus 73.53, 64.58, and 55.20 for the HC solver. The affine variant also offers a competitive faster operating point.

Ablations substantiate the effects of the displacement, early non-minimal refitting, filtering, and refinement. The paper states important limitations rather than presenting the approximation as universally reliable.

Reproducibility is strong in principle: the construction uses standard solvers, principal hyperparameters are specified and validated, detailed supplementary experiments are included, and code and data releases are identified.
weaknesses: The main attribution and comparison weakness is that refinement and filtering are generic post-processing steps. Several headline speed-accuracy plots compare proposed +R/+F variants against plain 5pt+P3P and unrefined HC. Although Table 2 includes an enhanced 5pt+P3P baseline, matched fixed-budget curves are absent, and HC+R is not evaluated even though the same four-point objective appears applicable. Since the unrefined mean-point solvers are often only comparable to, or worse than, 5pt+P3P, the claimed solver-level advantage is not fully isolated.

Against the matched 5pt+P3P+R+F+ENM baseline in Table 2, the best mean-point method improves AUC@10 by only 0.94, 0.64, and 0.31 points while taking roughly 1.7–2 times longer. Confidence intervals or repeated-run variability are not reported, making the significance of these small margins unclear.

The theoretical justification is limited. The triangle bound can be very loose and provides no pose-error or success-probability guarantee. Moreover, the supplementary text states that the distance to the fixed epipolar line is equal to the maximum centroid-to-vertex distance; the argument establishes only an upper bound as written.

Some implementation-critical choices are insufficiently specified or analyzed, including selection of the three points forming the centroid, choice and ordering of the initial camera pair, and conversion of the estimated affine fundamental matrix into poses for triangulation. The method is asymmetric, yet sensitivity to camera or point permutations is not reported.

The real-data study uses only SuperPoint-LightGlue correspondences and is dominated by landmark-style imagery, so robustness to other noise distributions, matchers, indoor sequences, and forward-motion configurations remains uncertain. Presentation-only issues include dense variant nomenclature and repeated references to a nonexistent '+C' modification where '+F' appears intended.

strengths: The paper offers a simple, original, and practically useful approach to a notoriously difficult geometric problem: it constructs an approximate fifth correspondence from four three-view tracks and reuses efficient, established 5-point and P3P solvers. This substantially lowers implementation complexity relative to the homotopy-continuation approach. The assessment covers the complete manuscript and supplement. :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/run-20260914-03/reviews/cvpr2025--gpt56_sol/review-experiment-31knlojk/call-6b1612ba72d24822b036b7f5dc0a6e15/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"}

The solver design is coherent and thoughtfully engineered. The mean-point construction supplies a generically additional perspective constraint, while the shifted hypotheses, early non-minimal refitting, fourth-point filtering, and short LM refinement address complementary failure modes.

The empirical evaluation is unusually broad for a camera-geometry paper: 90,000 triplets from 18 scenes across three datasets, two RANSAC frameworks, several synthetic camera/noise configurations, an outlier study, threshold sensitivity, individual-scene results, and an alternative all-pairs pose metric.

The strongest method consistently improves accuracy. In PoseLib, 4p3v(M±δ)+R+F+ENM obtains AUC@10 values of 77.14, 66.95, and 57.42 on PhotoTourism, Cambridge, and Aachen, compared with 73.53, 64.58, and 55.20 for 4p3v(HC). Its gains also persist under GC-RANSAC, where they are more substantial relative to 5pt+P3P.

The ablations support the importance of refinement and show limited sensitivity to the selected shift and LM iteration count. Public code and data links, thresholds, iteration schedules, validation separation, and CPU information provide a good basis for reproducibility.
weaknesses: Materially, the theoretical support for the central approximation is limited. The lemma only establishes that the epipolar line intersects the projected triangle, bounding the mean point's residual by its maximum distance to a triangle vertex. This bound can be arbitrarily large relative to the inlier threshold and gives no control over essential-matrix conditioning or pose error; the method consequently remains an empirically supported heuristic.

The improvements over the strongest enhanced 5pt+P3P baseline are modest in the main PoseLib evaluation: AUC@10 rises only from 76.20 to 77.14 on PhotoTourism, 66.31 to 66.95 on Cambridge, and 57.11 to 57.42 on Aachen, while runtime approximately doubles. Thus, the evidence supports a favorable speed-accuracy frontier, rather than an unqualified accuracy-and-speed dominance.

The runtime comparison with 4p3v(HC) is not fully fair. The supplement states that approximately 45 ms of network-data loading occurs once per RANSAC run; retaining those fixed data in memory across triplets would substantially shift the HC speed-accuracy curves. Accuracy comparisons remain valid, but some practical runtime claims are weakened.

No confidence intervals, repeated random seeds, or significance tests are reported. Given the sub-one-point AUC margins over the enhanced 5pt+P3P baseline, the 5,000 triplets per scene reduce sampling uncertainty but do not establish that all small differences exceed RANSAC-run variability.

Generality is incompletely tested. All real experiments use SuperPoint-LightGlue tracks consistent across all three views and a fixed decomposition through the first two cameras. There is no study of feature/matcher dependence, camera-order permutations, or partial-visibility tracks, although the competing (5,5,3) baseline can naturally exploit points not visible in every view.

As a presentation/reproducibility refinement, the manuscript should specify how the affine fundamental matrix is converted into metric camera poses, the correspondence-ordering policy, and the precise LM parameterization. Table 7 also reports exactly identical Cambridge results and runtimes for distinct A- and M-based variants, suggesting a copy or reporting error. These issues should be clarified but do not overturn the extensive main evidence.

strengths: The paper addresses a difficult and practically relevant three-view geometry problem with an appealingly simple idea: construct an approximate fifth correspondence from four three-view matches, then reuse efficient 5-point and P3P solvers. This is original enough in context and substantially easier to implement than prior homotopy-based approaches.

The method is technically plausible and thoughtfully engineered. The mean-point construction, shifted-point hypotheses, early non-minimal refitting, fourth-point filtering, and two-step LM refinement form a coherent RANSAC pipeline; the supplementary analysis explains why the mean point supplies a generically additional perspective constraint.

The evaluation is unusually broad for a geometric solver paper: 90,000 triplets from 18 scenes across PhotoTourism, Cambridge Landmarks, and Aachen; PoseLib and GC-RANSAC; synthetic camera-geometry and noise studies; semi-synthetic outlier tests; threshold sensitivity; per-scene results; ablations; and an alternative pose metric including all camera pairs.

Results consistently support practical usefulness. In PoseLib, 4p3v(M±δ)+R+F+ENM improves AUC@10 over the enhanced 5pt+P3P baseline from 76.20 to 77.14, 66.31 to 66.95, and 57.11 to 57.42 on the three benchmarks, respectively, while giving larger improvements over 4p3v(HC). Fixed-budget curves also support a favorable speed-accuracy trade-off.

Reproducibility is comparatively strong: source code and data are linked, key settings such as δ=0.08, two LM iterations, matching pipeline, thresholds, hardware, and RANSAC configurations are reported, and both solver-only and end-to-end runtimes are provided.
weaknesses: Material concern: the generic fourth-point refinement and filtering are not applied uniformly to all competitors. In particular, 4p3v(HC) is always reported without +R/+F even though its relaxed fourth observation could in principle initialize the same full-correspondence refinement; GC-RANSAC also lacks a 5pt+P3P+R/+F comparison. Since the ablations identify +R as the largest improvement, the experiments do not completely isolate the advantage of the proposed hypothesis generator.

The advantage over the equally enhanced 5pt+P3P baseline is modest: the AUC@10 gains above are 0.94, 0.64, and 0.31 points, while the strongest variant takes approximately 1.7-2.0 times the full PoseLib runtime and its raw solver is about 2.8 times slower. No confidence intervals, repeated-seed variation, or significance analysis are supplied for these relatively small differences.

The theoretical guarantee is weak and stated imprecisely. Lemma 1 only shows that the relevant epipolar line intersects the projected triangle, giving a distance upper bound that scales with triangle size and no bound on pose error. The subsequent statement that the distance to the line is equal to the maximum distance to the triangle vertices should be an inequality in general. Degenerate cases for the claimed independence of the mean-point constraint are also not characterized.

Evaluation uses only SuperPoint-LightGlue triplets that are consistent across all three images and mostly static landmark scenes. Results with other matchers, realistic structured outliers, dynamic scenes, or partial-visibility correspondence patterns are absent, so the practical generality of the reported advantage remains uncertain.

Some standalone implementation details are underspecified, including which three of the four samples define the mean point and P3P instance, pose/scale parameterization and residual aggregation during refinement, and precise solution and cheirality filtering. Moreover, the Cambridge portion of Table 7 contains exactly duplicated multi-metric rows for affine- and mean-based variants, suggesting a copy or reporting error that should be resolved.

strengths: The paper addresses the difficult and practically relevant four-points-in-three-calibrated-views problem. Its central idea—constructing a mean-point pseudo-correspondence and composing established 5-point and P3P solvers—is simple, plausibly original, and easy to integrate into robust-estimation systems.

The empirical evaluation is unusually extensive for a geometric-solver paper: 90,000 triplets across 18 scenes and three datasets, two RANSAC frameworks, per-scene results, runtime–accuracy curves, an alternative all-camera-pairs metric, and studies of noise, outliers, camera geometry, thresholds, delta, and refinement iterations.

The proposed pipelines consistently outperform the prior HC solver. In PoseLib, the strongest variant reaches AUC@10 of 77.14/66.95/57.42 on PhotoTourism/Cambridge/Aachen, versus 73.53/64.58/55.20 for HC. GC-RANSAC experiments provide independent support for the practical value of the approach.

The paper includes meaningful ablations and does not hide that the unrefined affine approximation performs poorly or that performance can be scene-dependent. Reporting multiple speed–accuracy operating points is more informative than claiming value solely from one best score.

Reproducibility is supported by publicly identified source code and archived data, while the implementation builds mostly on standard PoseLib, 5-point, P3P, and RANSAC components. The manuscript itself was inspected in full. :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/run-20260914-03/reviews/cvpr2025--gpt56_sol/review-experiment-b2tu322b/call-f77b3cc000dc4898a6525e42ccba99dc/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"}
weaknesses: The theoretical justification is limited. The geometric lemma only supplies a potentially loose image-space bound and gives no bound on pose error or solver success. It also needs explicit visibility/nondegeneracy assumptions, and the text claims an equality with the maximum vertex distance where the proof establishes only an upper bound. The claimed independence of the mean-point constraint should likewise be qualified as generic.

The comparison with HC is not fully controlled: the strongest proposed methods include refinement and filtering, and the ablation shows refinement is important, yet HC is reported without an analogous post-estimation refinement. ENM may be structurally inapplicable to HC, but refinement of an HC three-camera initialization appears applicable and is not evaluated.

Against the more fairly enhanced 5pt+P3P baseline, the best PoseLib AUC@10 gains are only 0.94, 0.64, and 0.31 points on the three datasets, while that variant is approximately 1.7–2 times slower. No repeated-run variability or confidence intervals are reported, so the significance of these small differences is uncertain, although matched-runtime curves and GC-RANSAC results remain favorable.

Several implementation-critical details are insufficiently specified in the manuscript: how the affine fundamental matrix is converted into a valid calibrated pose, which three of the four correspondences define the mean point and P3P instance, handling of point/view ordering, the exact three-view refinement objective and parameterization, and filtering/ENM thresholds. Released code mitigates but does not remove this standalone reproducibility issue.

The evaluation uses one SuperPoint–LightGlue triplet-generation pipeline, known calibration, and triplets already having at least ten three-way matches. It therefore does not establish robustness to calibration error, alternative correspondence pipelines, or the scarce-track cases where requiring four rather than five correspondences may be most valuable. These are meaningful scope limitations, but they do not outweigh the supported practical contribution.

strengths: The paper addresses a difficult and practically relevant geometric-estimation problem with a notably simple idea: constructing an approximate fifth correspondence from three point-track centroids and combining standard 5pt and P3P solvers. The resulting method is substantially easier to implement than prior specialized 4p3v solvers.

The empirical evaluation is unusually broad: 90,000 triplets from 18 real scenes across PhotoTourism, Cambridge Landmarks, and Aachen, plus synthetic noise, geometry, threshold, and outlier studies. Results are also reported with two RANSAC frameworks and an alternative metric covering all three camera pairs.

The strongest proposed configuration improves the reported PoseLib AUC@10 over the strengthened 5pt+P3P baseline on all three datasets (77.14 versus 76.20, 66.95 versus 66.31, and 57.42 versus 57.11). Faster affine-based variants provide competitive Pareto points, so the contribution is potentially useful even though the absolute gains are modest.

Ablations cover the mean-point perturbation, early non-minimal refitting, fourth-point filtering and refinement, RANSAC thresholds, and refinement iterations. Public code and data links further support reproducibility.
weaknesses: The central mean-point solver without ENM/refinement is worse than ordinary 5pt+P3P on all three PoseLib aggregates, while the affine solver can fail severely. Most final gains arise only after generic refitting and local refinement. The paper lacks controls using alternative pseudo-correspondences or equally budgeted hypothesis diversification, making it difficult to isolate the benefit of the proposed mean construction.

The strongest comparison is incomplete. The main speed-accuracy curves omit 5pt+P3P+R+F, and the GC-RANSAC study omits R/F for the baseline even though the manuscript demonstrates that these operations apply to it and materially improve it. The remaining advantage over the strengthened baseline is small and is reported without confidence intervals or paired significance analysis.

The runtime comparison with 4p3v(HC) is not implementation-neutral: the manuscript reports a roughly 45 ms model-loading cost once per RANSAC, although this could normally be cached across many triplets. Solver-only timings actually favor HC over 4p3v(M) and especially 4p3v(M±δ), weakening claims of a definitive speed-accuracy advantage.

The theoretical result provides only a loose, triangle-size-dependent bound on pseudo-correspondence epipolar error and no bound on pose error or probability of generating a useful hypothesis. Moreover, the supplementary text incorrectly states an equality between point-to-line distance and the maximum distance to the triangle vertices; only an inequality is justified. Important degeneracies such as small baseline, nearly collinear samples, and planar configurations are not characterized.

All real-data matches are required to form complete three-view tracks. This favors the proposed four-track formulation and does not evaluate the natural advantage of the (5,5,3) baseline, which can draw its two additional correspondences from pairwise-only matches. Practical claims therefore do not cover common partial-visibility regimes.

Several implementation-critical details are underspecified, including conversion of the affine fundamental matrix to calibrated poses, selection/order of the three points used for the centroid and P3P, handling of multiple 5pt/P3P roots, and the exact refinement residual and parameterization. In addition, GC-RANSAC Table 7 repeats entire aggregate rows for distinct affine and mean-point variants on Cambridge, which warrants verification.
